funcs.CHAR: CHAR(n USING utf8mb4) reads n as a byte sequence in that charset, not as a code point: CHAR(233 USING utf8mb4) is NULL because 0xE9 alone is not valid UTF-8, where SEL says the character is e-acute
funcs.CODE: ORD returns the first character's bytes read as an integer, not its code point; SEL's CODE is a code point
funcs.RREPLACE: SEL replacement syntax is $0-$9 and MariaDB's is \1; rewriting one into the other is only possible when the replacement is a literal, which the map cannot express

skel.join: GROUP_CONCAT does not specify an order without an ORDER BY, and a relation binding has no key to order by; SEL's JOIN concatenates in insertion order

notes.purpose: The spellings MariaDB and MySQL agree on. Neither is a parent of the other: MariaDB is the reference this project tests against, and a reference dialect should not inherit from one nobody has exercised. Version-gated entries belong in the leaves, since `since` is compared against the target's version.
notes.textEscape: The backslash entry is not optional. Under the default sql_mode both servers treat \ as an escape inside a string literal, so a text value containing one must double it. PostgreSQL and SQLite do not, and their documents omit this key.
notes.numericCast: DECIMAL(65,10) rather than ansi's DECIMAL(38,10): 65 is the maximum precision both servers support, and SEL numbers have no width limit of their own, so taking all of it is the least surprising choice.
notes.TRIM: SEL strips space, tab, CR and LF. TRIM(BOTH x FROM s) takes one string rather than a character set, so it cannot express that; REGEXP_REPLACE can. The doubled backslashes survive the string literal and reach the regex engine as \t, \r and \n.
notes.ENCODE_BASE64: TO_BASE64 wraps its output with a newline every 76 characters. SEL's does not, so the newlines are stripped. The result is then exactly the standard padded alphabet SEL specifies.
notes.DECODE_BASE64: FROM_BASE64 accepts whitespace and is lenient where SEL requires padding and rejects any invalid character. It decodes valid input identically; it is the invalid input the two disagree about.
notes.CODE: ORD('e-acute') is 50089 on a utf8mb4 column — the two UTF-8 bytes read as a big-endian integer — where SEL says 233. ASCII agrees by accident, which is worse than disagreeing, so this is refused rather than caveated.
notes.CHAR: The inverse of CODE and refused for the inverse reason. Verified against MariaDB 11.8: SELECT CHAR(233 USING utf8mb4) is NULL. Code points below 128 would work, but an entry that is right for ASCII and silently wrong above it is the worst of the three options.
notes.sql_mode: This document assumes the default sql_mode, specifically that NO_BACKSLASH_ESCAPES is off. Two things depend on it: textEscape doubles backslashes inside string literals, and the TRIM family's regex escapes reach the engine as \t, \r and \n only because the literal parser consumes one backslash of each pair. A deployment running NO_BACKSLASH_ESCAPES needs a derived dialect overriding both. ENCODE_BASE64 deliberately uses CHAR(10) and CHAR(13) instead, since REPLACE is not a regex and had nothing to gain from the assumption.
